title: How to Evaluate RAG Retrieval in 2026: Question Sets, Metrics That Mislead, and a Practical Recipe
author: Muhammad Hussnain Jamil
summary: Many RAG failures get blamed on "the LLM" when the generator never had a chance: the passage it needed was not in the context, or it was buried under near-duplicates. Retrieval deserves its own evaluation. It is also easy to get wrong, because the score depends on what you call "relevant", how you built the questions, which k you chose and how many questions you asked. This article covers the whole chain as it stands in late 2026: labelled question sets (including synthetic ones and their traps), the metrics and where each misleads, statistical noise, lexical versus paraphrased questions, evaluating chunking, hybrid search and rerankers, LLM-as-judge and its documented biases, end-to-end metrics, current tools and benchmarks, and a recipe you can apply this week. Numbers of my own come from small, reproducible experiments in my public lab repo, applied-llm-lab . They show how metrics behave; they are not a benchmark. Why evaluate retrieval on its own Retrieval quality changes answer quality in ways the generator cannot fix. Google researchers defined sufficient context as context that "contains all the necessary information to provide a definitive answer" and found that insufficient context can make models less likely to abstain: for one model the incorrect-answer rate rose from 10.2% with no context to 66.1% with insufficient context [2]. A weak retriever can actively produce confident wrong answers. Serious RAG work measures the retriever directly. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval write-up used "1 minus recall@20" and reported failure rates falling from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings, to 2.9% with contextual BM25 added, and to 1.9% with reranking [1], all measured before any answer was generated. Retrieval-only metrics are also cheaper, deterministic once labels are fixed, and they localise problems: if recall@20 is fine but answers are wrong, look at the prompt or generator; if recall@20 is poor, no prompt will save you. Step zero: decide what "relevant" means Every retrieval metric compares a ranked list against a set of relevant items. Before choosing a metric, decide what the unit of relevance is: Unit Example label Good for Weakness Document ID doc_17 Classic IR benchmarks, small docs Says nothing about chunking Chunk ID doc_17#chunk_3 Fast regression tests on one fixed index Labels break when you re-chunk Text span / fact "Each chunk keeps the file name and page number as metadata" Comparing chunkers, rerankers, hybrid setups Needs span matching logic Claims / nuggets List of atomic facts from a reference answer Multi-fact questions, end-to-end analysis Needs an LLM or human to check entailment Tokens Exact character ranges of relevant text Measuring chunk efficiency More engineering; unusual in tools Chroma's chunking study notes that document-level benchmarks like MTEB and BEIR "cannot take chunking into account" and measures token-wise precision, recall and intersection over union instead [18]. RAGChecker works at claim level: claim recall is the share of ground-truth claims entailed by the retrieved chunks [19]. In my lab a chunk counts as the answer chunk only if it contains the whole answer fact. With fixed-size chunks some facts are cut in half, so for those questions no chunk can be relevant and the miss is guaranteed. Relevance definition and chunker interact, and the metric reflects both. Building the labelled question set Questions come from three sources, in decreasing order of realism: real user queries from logs or tickets, subject-matter experts, and LLM-generated (synthetic) questions. A useful record holds the question, the relevant span(s) or claims, optional graded relevance, a short reference answer, and tags such as lexical / paraphrased , single-hop / multi-hop , has-identifier and unanswerable . Tags let you see that a change helped one slice and hurt another. Label spans or claims rather than chunk IDs if you will ever compare chunkers: chunk-ID labels silently become wrong when you re-chunk. Synthetic question sets: useful, but biased in known ways Generation is now a standard feature. Ragas builds a knowledge graph from your documents, then synthesizers produce single-hop or multi-hop, specific or abstract queries with configurable length and style [9]. Langfuse documents routes via Ragas, DeepEval's synthesizer, or a custom loop writing one question per chunk [17]. Chroma's chunking study shows careful filtering: queries whose evidence excerpts were not exact matches in the corpus were rejected, and near-duplicate or weakly related queries were removed with embedding thresholds [18]. The research on trusting synthetic sets is nuanced: Synthetic queries do not look like real ones. A September 2026 study found authentic queries averaged 6.8 words versus 15.7 for synthetic ones, real users concentrated on a few topics while synthetic questions spread evenly, and optimising on synthetic queries picked a hybrid retriever costing up to 8 times the latency of the fastest configuration, whose sparse half did not help short real queries [29]. Synthetic collections inflate absolute scores and favour their own model family. Rahmani et al. found GPT-4 more lenient than human assessors on borderline passages, scores generally higher on synthetic data, and systems from the generator's model family favoured; the bias matters most for absolute scores and less for relative comparisons [27]. Their earlier SIGIR 2024 paper showed synthetic test collections can be used reliably for retrieval evaluation [26]. Synthetic sets rank retrievers better than generators. Van Elburg et al. report that synthetic benchmarks "reliably rank the RAGs varying in terms of retriever configuration" but "do not consistently produce reliable RAG rankings when comparing generator architectures" [28]. Two more traps follow from how per-chunk generation works. A question written while looking at one chunk tends to reuse its vocabulary, which flatters lexical retrievers (measure this on your own set; see below). And it is answerable from exactly one chunk by construction, so multi-chunk and unanswerable questions are under-represented. Practical stance: use synthetic questions for coverage and for comparing retriever configurations, keep a smaller human-written or log-derived set as the arbiter, and report them separately. If they disagree about the winner, believe the real one. The metrics, precisely Here are the definitions most tools use. Let rank be the 1-based position of a relevant item, k the cutoff, and R the set of relevant items for one question. Every metric is averaged over questions. Metric Per-question definition Answers the question Hit rate@k (success@k) 1 if any relevant item is in the top k, else 0 "Did we find anything useful?" Recall@k relevant items in top k / |R| "How much of what is needed did we find?" Precision@k relevant items in top k / k "How much of the context is useful?" MRR@k 1 / rank of the first relevant item (0 if none in top k) "How high is the first useful item?" nDCG@k DCG@k / ideal DCG@k, with DCG = Σ gain / log2(rank + 1) "Are the most relevant items near the top?" (supports graded relevance) Context recall (LLM) reference-answer claims supported by the retrieved context / all claims Recall without labelled chunks Context precision (LLM) rank-weighted precision over chunks judged relevant Ranking quality without labelled chunks Notes on origins and variants: MRR comes from the TREC-8 QA track, where a question scored "the reciprocal of the rank at which the first correct response was returned," or 0 if none of the top five was correct [3]. nDCG was introduced by Järvelin and Kekäläinen for graded relevance with a rank discount [4]. With one binary relevant item it reduces to 1 / log2(rank + 1): 1.00 at rank 1, 0.63 at rank 2, 0.50 at rank 3. Haystack's nDCG evaluator uses ground-truth scores as graded relevance when present and binary relevance otherwise [15]. "Recall" is overloaded. Haystack's DocumentRecallEvaluator has single_hit (score 1 if any ground-truth document is retrieved, i.e. hit rate) and multi_hit (full score only if all are) [14]. Say which one you mean. Context precision is not one formula. In Ragas, the LLM-based version averages precision@k over the positions of chunks judged relevant, so ranking matters; the ID-based version is plain precision without rank weighting [5]. DeepEval's contextual precision also weights by position, judges against expected_output , and warns that scores from different evaluation modes are not comparable [10]. Context recall (Ragas, DeepEval) splits the reference answer into claims and checks which can be attributed to the retrieved context [6][11]; Ragas also has non-LLM and ID-based variants. DeepEval's contextual relevancy is reference-free: the share of statements in the retrieved context relevant to the input [12]. When each metric misleads Hit rate@k with a large k hides ranking. Hit@20 can stay flat while the relevant chunk slides from rank 1 to rank 15. That matters if the generator sees only the top 5, or handles long contexts unevenly: "Lost in the Middle" found performance "is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context" [38]. Chroma, by contrast, argues LLMs are relatively insensitive to position and down-weights nDCG-style metrics for RAG [18]. Both can hold for different models and context lengths, so report a rank-sensitive metric next to hit rate instead of picking one. MRR ignores everything after the first relevant item. For a question needing three facts from three chunks, MRR rewards one at rank 1 and is blind to the other two. Use recall@k or claim-level context recall for multi-fact questions. Precision@k is capped by the number of relevant items. With one relevant chunk, the best precision@5 is 0.20. Low precision matters when the extra chunks are distractors that pull the generator off course [2]. Incomplete labels punish novel retrievers. Unlabelled items count as irrelevant. BEIR found many datasets "subject to a lexical bias" from pooling with lexical systems; after missing TREC-COVID judgments were annotated, a dense retriever's nDCG@10 rose from 0.654 to 0.735, moving above BM25 [20]. Labels made by looking at BM25 results make new embedding models look worse. Chunk-level metrics are not comparable across chunkers. Larger chunks contain more facts, so they win hit rate almost by definition while wasting context. Chroma's token-level IoU exposes this: a recursive splitter at 800 tokens with 400 overlap (the chunking settings OpenAI Assistants used by default at the time of the study) scored an IoU of 1.5, against 6.9 for the same splitter at 200 tokens with no overlap, and reducing overlap improved IoU because overlap adds redundant tokens [18]. The same metric name gives different numbers in different tools. Rank-weighted versus unweighted context precision, single_hit versus multi_hit recall, LLM-judged versus ID-based: pin the tool, version and variant in your eval report. How the metrics behave on a toy set: my lab results The experiments in applied-llm-lab build a tiny pipeline from scratch: Day 01, chunking: fixed-size chunks cut sentences in half; sentence packing kept every sentence whole at a similar chunk size. Day 02, BM25 from scratch: on 5 questions, sentence-packed chunks put the whole fact in BM25's top result 5/5 times, versus 2/5 for fixed-size chunks (4/5 with overlap). Day 03, TF-IDF cosine with NumPy: the same hit counts as BM25 (5/5 with sentence chunks). On 3 paraphrased questions both scored 0/3, so paraphrases need learned embeddings. Day 04 added metrics: a 6-paragraph corpus about RAG pipelines and 12 questions, each asked in the document's own words ("original") and mostly in other words ("paraphrased"). The answer chunk is the one containing the whole fact. The harness core, in the same style: def first_relevant_rank ( ranked_chunks , fact , k = 5 ): """ 1-based rank of the first top-k chunk that holds the whole fact, or None. """ for rank , chunk in enumerate ( ranked_chunks [: k ], start = 1 ): if fact in " " . join ( chunk . split ()): # normalise whitespace before matching return rank return None def summarize ( ranks ): """ Average hit@1, hit@3 and reciprocal rank (MRR@5) over all questions. """ n = len ( ranks ) return { " hit@1 " : sum ( r == 1 for r in ranks ) / n , " hit@3 " : sum ( r is not None and r <= 3 for r in ranks ) / n , " mrr@5 " : sum ( 1 / r for r in ranks if r ) / n , } assert summarize ([ 1 , 2 , None ]) == { " hit@1 " : 1 / 3 , " hit@3 " : 2 / 3 , " mrr@5 " : 0.5 } BM25 and TF-IDF cosine gave identical numbers in every row, so the table shows one value per row: Chunking Questions hit@1 hit@3 MRR@5 Fixed size, 120 chars original 0.67 0.67 0.67 Fixed size, 120 chars paraphrased 0.50 0.58 0.53 Fixed 120 + 30 overlap original 0.83 0.83 0.83 Fixed 120 + 30 overlap paraphrased 0.42 0.67 0.54 Sentence packing, max 160 original 1.00 1.00 1.00 Sentence packing, max 160 paraphrased 0.83 0.83 0.83 What the toy set shows about the metrics: Hit@3 alone would call overlap a clear win on paraphrases (0.58 to 0.67). But hit@1 dropped from 0.50 to 0.42 and MRR barely moved (0.53 to 0.54). In each of the three rank-2 cases a neighbouring overlap chunk ranked first, and in two of them it held only part of the fact. Overlap creates near-duplicates that compete with the real answer chunk: "hit rate hides ranking" in miniature. Paraphrasing costs every configuration. The best chunker still lost 2 of 12. Per-question ranks from rerunning the script show both misses hinge on an abbreviation the text spells differently: "retrieval-augmented generation" versus "RAG", and "RRF" versus "reciprocal rank fusion". No shared terms, no lexical match. Two lexical scorers with different maths ranked identically. On a tiny corpus with short chunks, the differences between BM25 and TF-IDF cosine do not show up. Then the most important caveat. Statistical noise: one question in 12 is 0.08 With 12 questions, each question moves a score by 1/12 = 0.083. The gap between 0.42 and 0.50 hit@1 above is one question . Confidence intervals make this concrete. Using the Wilson score interval for a proportion: Hits / questions Point estimate 95% Wilson interval 8 / 12 0.67 0.39 to 0.86 10 / 12 0.83 0.55 to 0.95 12 / 12 1.00 0.76 to 1.00 83 / 100 0.83 0.74 to 0.89 250 / 300 0.83 0.79 to 0.87 The intervals for 8/12 and 12/12 overlap. Even the most dramatic result in my table, sentence packing beating fixed-size chunks 12/12 versus 8/12 on original questions, is not statistically convincing on its own: the four questions fixed-size missed were all hit by sentence packing, and none went the other way, which gives an exact two-sided McNemar (sign) test p-value of 2 × 0.5⁴ = 0.125. Three habits fix most of this: Use paired tests on the same questions. Smucker, Allan and Carterette found "little practical difference between the randomization, bootstrap, and t tests" for IR, preferred the randomization test, and argued Wilcoxon and sign tests should be discontinued for differences between means [39]. Miller's paper on error bars for LLM evals recommends inference on question-level paired differences, clustered standard errors when questions come in related groups (say, several generated from one document), and power analysis [40]. Size the set for the difference you care about. The 95% half-width for a proportion near 0.8 is roughly 1.96 × √(0.16 / n): about ±0.08 at n = 100 and ±0.04 at n = 400. A few dozen questions cannot detect a 3-point improvement. Report counts, not only ratios. "10/12" tells the reader what "0.83" hides. A paired randomization test needs only the standard library: import random def paired_randomization_test ( a , b , trials = 10_000 , seed = 0 ): """ Two-sided p-value for mean(a) - mean(b), flipping signs of per-question differences. """ diffs = [ x - y for x , y in zip ( a , b )] observed = abs ( sum ( diffs )) rng = random . Random ( seed ) extreme = sum ( abs ( sum ( d if rng . random () < 0.5 else - d for d in diffs )) >= observed for _ in range ( trials ) ) return ( extreme + 1 ) / ( trials + 1 ) Run on the per-question hit@1 scores of the sentence-packing and fixed-size rows above, it returns about 0.12, matching the exact test. If you prefer a library, ranx provides paired Student's t-test, Fisher's randomization test and Tukey's HSD alongside its metrics [42]. Lexical versus paraphrased questions Paraphrases test the gap between how documents are written and how users ask. Lexical retrievers win on exact identifiers; BEIR found BM25 "a robust baseline" that dense models often failed to beat zero-shot [20]. Dense retrievers handle different wording but have their own limits: Weller et al. prove the number of top-k subsets a single-vector embedding can return is bounded by its dimension, and built LIMIT, on which state-of-the-art embedders fail despite very simple queries [25]. Reasoning-heavy queries break both: on BRIGHT's 1,384 real queries, a model scoring 59.0 nDCG@10 on BEIR scored 18.3, and explicit reasoning about the query added up to 12.2 points [23]. For your own set: Stratify into lexical (shares key terms with the answer span), paraphrased, identifier lookups and multi-hop or reasoning questions, and report every metric per stratum. Measure lexical overlap automatically (share of question tokens found in the answer span) and compare the synthetic and real splits. A high-overlap set makes BM25 look better than it will be in production. Write paraphrases deliberately , including abbreviations, synonyms and user jargon. My two universal misses were both abbreviation mismatches. Evaluating chunking, hybrid search and rerankers Chunking. Use span or claim labels so one question set fits every chunker. Report hit@k with a rank-sensitive metric and a cost measure (tokens sent to the generator, or token-level IoU [18]); otherwise bigger chunks always win. If you can, fix the context budget in tokens , not in number of chunks. Hybrid search. Reciprocal rank fusion scores each document as Σ 1 / (k + rank) over the input rankings, with k = 60 fixed in a pilot study where "the choice was not critical" [41]. Fusion helps only if the inputs make different mistakes; my BM25 and TF-IDF ranked identically, so fusing them would add nothing. On FreshStack, a 2025 benchmark built from Stack Overflow questions and technical documentation, fusing four retrievers beat each one on most metrics and topics [24]. Report latency next to quality: the sparse half of a hybrid can help long synthetic questions but not short real ones, at several times the latency [29]. Rerankers. Evaluate the stages separately: the first stage needs high recall at the candidate depth you rerank (Anthropic reranked 150 candidates down to 20 [1]), the reranker needs good nDCG@k or MRR@k at the depth the generator sees. Rerankers do not always help: on FreshStack one improved some topics and lowered scores for some dense and fusion runs on others [24]. LLM-as-judge for retrieval Labelling relevance by hand does not scale, so LLM judges are now everywhere: they power LLM-based context precision and recall, and they label pools for benchmarks. The case for them is real. Thomas et al. found LLMs as accurate as human labellers in their experiments, and LLM labelling in production at Bing proved "not just more efficient but more accurate than the status quo" [30]. UMBRELA reproduced this with GPT-4o on TREC Deep Learning 2019 to 2023 and supported assessments in the TREC 2024 RAG track [31]. The biases are real too: Bias Evidence Mitigation Leniency / overrating Consistent overrating, often with high confidence, sensitive to passage length and lexical cues [34]; GPT-4 more lenient than humans on borderline passages [27] Calibrate on a human-labelled subset; strict, aspect-based prompts Keyword stuffing GPT-4 with a basic prompt labelled about 26% of random nonsense passages perfectly relevant once the query string was inserted [32] Test with adversarial passages first Instruction injection A planted sentence claiming the passage holds the answer fooled several models [32] Treat retrieved text as untrusted; delimit it Self-preference, circularity Generator's model family favoured [27]; using the judging LLM as a reranker distorts rankings [33] Judge from a different model family Position, verbosity General LLM-judge biases [35] Randomise order; judge one chunk at a time Prompt sensitivity Quality "varies unpredictably with simple paraphrases" [30] Freeze and version prompt and model Alaofi et al. also found that agreement scores such as Cohen's kappa did not reliably predict how gullible a judge was [32], so "kappa looks fine" is not enough. Clarke and Dietz argue LLM-based assessment still cannot replace human assessment, especially for benchmarks meant to guide future research [33]. A practical middle ground is what ARES formalised: an automatic judge at scale, corrected by a small human-labelled set through prediction-powered inference, using "only a few hundred human annotations" [36]. Retrieval-only versus end-to-end metrics Faithfulness (Ragas): share of answer claims inferable from the retrieved context [7]. No reference needed, but it measures grounding, not correctness: a faithful answer from the wrong passage is still wrong. Answer correctness (Ragas): an F1-style claim overlap with the reference answer, combined with semantic similarity [8]. Nugget evaluation (TREC 2024 RAG track): answers scored by the atomic facts they cover. Automated nugget evaluation agrees strongly with human-based variants at run level, but per-topic agreement, which you need to diagnose individual failures, is not yet established [37]. Read both kinds together: Retrieval Answer Likely cause Good Good Working as intended Good Bad Generator, prompt, context ordering or context length Bad Good Model answered from parametric knowledge; fragile, and not grounded Bad Bad Fix retrieval first The "bad retrieval, good answer" cell is why end-to-end metrics alone are not enough: on public-knowledge questions the generator can mask a broken retriever, which stops working the moment questions concern your private documents. Tools and benchmarks in late 2026 Tool / benchmark What it gives you for retrieval Watch out for Ragas LLM-based, non-LLM and ID-based context precision and recall; faithfulness; testset generation [5][6][9] Legacy metric API slated for deprecation in 0.4 and removal in 1.0 [5]; pin versions DeepEval Contextual precision, recall and relevancy as test-case metrics [10][11][12] Scores from different evaluation modes are not comparable [10] Langfuse Datasets, experiments, scores, LLM-as-judge evaluators, annotation queues for human labels; Ragas integration [16][17] It is the platform; metric definitions come from what you plug in Haystack Statistical MRR, MAP, nDCG and recall evaluators plus LLM-based ones [13][14][15] Check single_hit versus multi_hit ranx Fast IR metrics, paired significance tests, 20+ fusion methods including RRF [42] Needs run/qrels formatted data BEIR 18 datasets, 9 tasks, zero-shot retrieval [20] Lexical bias in judgments MMTEB / MTEB 500+ tasks across 250+ languages; MTEB(eng, v2) designed as zero-shot [21] Leaderboard rank is not your corpus RTEB Retrieval-focused, open plus private datasets to expose overfitting; NDCG@10 default; 20 languages, enterprise domains [22] Beta BRIGHT Reasoning-intensive retrieval [23] Very different from FAQ-style RAG FreshStack Technical-docs retrieval with nugget-based α-nDCG@10, coverage@20, recall@50 [24] Five topics LIMIT Stress test for single-vector embedding limits [25] Deliberately simple queries; a stress test, not a target Public benchmarks are for shortlisting embedding models and rerankers. RTEB exists precisely because public scores can overstate real-world performance through train-test overlap [22]. The decision should come from your own labelled set. A practical evaluation recipe Define relevance as spans or claims , not chunk IDs, and write it down. Start with real or expert-written questions , labelled with spans, a reference answer and stratum tags, including some unanswerable ones. Size it with the interval arithmetic above: around 100 detects only large differences. Add synthetic questions for coverage with filtering (exact-match evidence, deduplication, relevance threshold) in a separate split, and compare its length and lexical overlap with the real split. Freeze the setup : corpus snapshot, question-set version, tool versions, judge model and prompt. Report a small panel per stratum : hit@k at the generator's k, MRR@k or nDCG@k, recall@N at the reranker's candidate depth, plus tokens in context and latency. Report counts and 95% intervals ; compare configurations with a paired randomization or bootstrap test. Change one thing at a time : chunker, retriever, fusion, reranker. Evaluate first stage and reranker separately. Validate any LLM judge against human labels and adversarial passages, using a different model family from your generator. Run end-to-end metrics too and read them with the 2×2 table above. Read individual failures. On the toy set, the abbreviation pattern is visible only in per-question ranks, not in the averages. Feed production queries back into the real split so the set follows your users, not your generator. Checklist [ ] Relevance unit (span, claim, chunk, document) documented [ ] Real or expert questions are the decision set; synthetic questions a separate split [ ] Questions tagged: lexical / paraphrased / identifier / multi-hop / unanswerable [ ] Synthetic split checked for length, lexical overlap and topic coverage [ ] One presence metric (hit@k or recall@k) plus one rank metric (MRR or nDCG) [ ] k matches what the generator or reranker receives [ ] Metric variant and tool version pinned [ ] Per-stratum counts with 95% intervals; paired tests for comparisons [ ] Context-cost metric for chunking comparisons [ ] LLM judge validated on human labels and adversarial passages [ ] Individual failures reviewed, not just averages What I'm testing next Next in the lab: hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, measured with the same Day 04 harness, and a learned-embedding retriever on the paraphrased set. Because BM25 and TF-IDF cosine ranked identically on this corpus, fusing those two alone is unlikely to change anything; the paraphrased questions, including the two abbreviation misses, are where a learned-embedding retriever should make the difference. With only 12 questions, I will read any change there as a direction, not a result. If you evaluate retrieval in production, I would like to know which metric panel you settled on and how many questions it took before the numbers stopped moving. title: 48-Hour Field Notes: I Compared Two Runs Across Two Days Without Checking Which Model Served Them
author: Taylor Wang
summary: Two runs, forty-eight hours apart, and a latency drop big enough that I started writing the summary before the second log had finished flushing. Then I printed the one metadata column I had been ignoring since day one. Is that a measurement bug, or is it a discipline bug wearing a lab coat? This is another entry in a small series where I break my own tooling over two days and write down the damage while it still stings. The target this time was a prompt-variance probe I wanted to run on free capacity, because requesting a budget line takes longer than building the thing. The Setup: One Question, Two Unnamed Unknowns The question was narrow. After I rewrote a system prompt, did identical inputs produce identical outputs more often than before? That is a variance question, not a leaderboard question, and it needs volume rather than expensive tokens. I used MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option so the loop could run without a spend approval, which is the entire reason day two existed at all. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The availability claims are the operator's; everything about the harness below is mine to defend or retract. Before writing a line of code I listed the unknowns I was not measuring, and both of them came back to bite me within the window: Which model revision actually served each request, and whether that stayed constant. How long a long-running process survives on shared, free compute before something reclaims it. Neither is exotic. Both are the kind of thing you only notice when you decide you want to publish a number. Day 1: The Harness That Saved Me From Myself I refused to write a benchmark first. I wrote a logger, because a benchmark without raw rows is a story I am telling myself. Every request appends one JSON line, and nothing is aggregated until the log is closed. # probe.py import hashlib , json , time from pathlib import Path from datetime import datetime , timezone LOG = Path ( ' runs/probe.jsonl ' ) LOG . parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) def fp ( obj ) -> str : blob = json . dumps ( obj , sort_keys = True ). encode ( ' utf-8 ' ) return hashlib . sha256 ( blob ). hexdigest ()[: 12 ] def probe ( client , prompt : str , run_id : str , repeat : int ) -> dict : t0 = time . perf_counter () resp = client . chat ( prompt = prompt , temperature = 0 , seed = 7 ) record = { ' run_id ' : run_id , ' repeat ' : repeat , ' prompt_fp ' : fp ({ ' p ' : prompt }), ' text_fp ' : fp ({ ' t ' : resp . text }), ' model_field ' : resp . meta . get ( ' model ' ), ' revision_field ' : resp . meta . get ( ' revision ' ) or resp . meta . get ( ' system_fingerprint ' ), ' tokens_in ' : resp . usage . get ( ' input_tokens ' ), ' tokens_out ' : resp . usage . get ( ' output_tokens ' ), ' latency_ms ' : round (( time . perf_counter () - t0 ) * 1000 , 1 ), ' utc ' : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). isoformat (), } with LOG . open ( ' a ' , encoding = ' utf-8 ' ) as fh : fh . write ( json . dumps ( record ) + ' \n ' ) return record Two details are load-bearing and easy to skip. The text_fp field hashes the raw output text so I can count distinct answers instead of eyeballing them, and revision_field reads whatever identifier the vendor echoes back, which differs per SDK. If your client library exposes no such field, that absence is itself a finding you should write down. The probe loop is deliberately boring: one prompt, twenty repeats, fixed temperature and seed, append-only log. Boring loops are the only ones I trust after 5pm. mkdir -p runs python probe.py --run day1 --repeats 20 Day 2: The Log Disagreed With My Summary I reran the same command the next morning, changed one file, and ran the analyzer before reading any average. The first line it printed was a refusal, not a p50. # analyze.py import json , statistics from collections import defaultdict from pathlib import Path rows = [ json . loads ( l ) for l in Path ( ' runs/probe.jsonl ' ). read_text (). splitlines () if l . strip ()] by_key = defaultdict ( list ) for r in rows : by_key [( r [ ' run_id ' ], r [ ' model_field ' ], r [ ' revision_field ' ])]. append ( r ) for key , rs in by_key . items (): lat = sorted ( r [ ' latency_ms ' ] for r in rs ) p95 = lat [ max ( 0 , int ( len ( lat ) * 0.95 ) - 1 )] outs = { r [ ' text_fp ' ] for r in rs } print ( f ' { key } n= { len ( rs ) } p50= { statistics . median ( lat ) } ms p95= { p95 } ms distinct_outputs= { len ( outs ) } ' ) revs = {( r [ ' model_field ' ], r [ ' revision_field ' ]) for r in rows } if len ( revs ) > 1 : raise SystemExit ( f ' STOP: { len ( revs ) } revisions in one log; do not compare across them ' ) That guard is the whole lesson. My day-one rows and day-two rows were grouped under different revision identifiers, which means the two "runs" were different systems wearing the same prompt. The numbers I was about to quote described a change of supplier, not a change of my prompt. What the dry run prints The digits below come from a stubbed client that fabricates responses, so read the shape and ignore the values. Real logs from your own endpoint should replace them before any claim leaves your draft folder. ('day1', 'stub-model', 'rev-a') n=20 p50=812.0ms p95=1490.0ms distinct_outputs=1 ('day2', 'stub-model', 'rev-b') n=20 p50=604.5ms p95=1102.0ms distinct_outputs=3 STOP: 2 revisions in one log; do not compare across them The distinct_outputs column matters more than the milliseconds, honestly. One stable answer on day one and three different answers on day two is a variance signal, and a variance signal that arrives alongside an identifier change is not attributable to my prompt. The Second Break: Free Compute Does Not Owe You Continuity Somewhere in the middle of the run my process stopped existing, and I only know that because the log ended mid-batch rather than at repeat twenty. Shared or free capacity is not a contract, so the fix is not a longer timeout; the fix is a job that can be picked up. The runner below is at-least-once by design, which is fine here because the probe is read-only. Every finished item is flushed with os.fsync so an abrupt stop loses at most the item in flight, and the resume path skips anything already marked ok . # runner.py import json , os from pathlib import Path STATE = Path ( ' runs/state.jsonl ' ) def load_done () -> set : if not STATE . exists (): return set () done = set () for line in STATE . read_text (). splitlines (): if line . strip (): rec = json . loads ( line ) if rec . get ( ' status ' ) == ' ok ' : done . add ( rec [ ' item_id ' ]) return done def append_state ( item_id : str , status : str , ** extra ) -> None : line = json . dumps ({ ' item_id ' : item_id , ' status ' : status , ** extra }) + ' \n ' with STATE . open ( ' a ' , encoding = ' utf-8 ' ) as fh : fh . write ( line ) fh . flush () os . fsync ( fh . fileno ()) def run ( items , handler ) -> None : done = load_done () for item in items : if item [ ' id ' ] in done : continue try : append_state ( item [ ' id ' ], ' ok ' , result = handler ( item )) except Exception as exc : append_state ( item [ ' id ' ], ' error ' , error = repr ( exc )) Restarting is then just the same command, and the log tells you how much was real work versus replay: python runner.py --queue runs/queue.jsonl wc -l runs/state.jsonl The Decision Table I Now Keep in the Repo After two days of this I wrote down when pinning matters, because I will absolutely forget by next quarter. The table is short on purpose. Situation Verify revision identifier? Rerun both sides? Note Same-day prompt iteration Record only No Compare within one revision bucket Comparing two calendar days Mandatory Yes, if identifiers differ Never quote across buckets Changing temperature or seed Record only Yes The setting is part of the treatment Latency claims Record only Yes Measure client-side, include queue time Any shared or free compute Record only Depends Assume interruption, checkpoint every item Publishing a number Mandatory Yes Include the raw log or drop the claim What I Would Repeat, and What I Would Not What I would repeat without hesitation: the JSONL-first habit, the analyzer that exits non-zero instead of printing a misleading mean, and the fsync on state writes. Each of those cost me maybe fifteen minutes and saved a day. What I would not repeat: starting the probe before deciding what a valid comparison even looks like. I recorded the model identifier from the very first request and still did not put a guard on it until the second day, which is a genuinely embarrassing order of operations. Finally, the boring one. I should have run the full loop end to end against two synthetic items before spending any window on real work. If you cannot resume from a killed process in under a minute of wall time, you are not ready to start a multi-day run on capacity you do not control. Limitations, and Who Should Skip This This workflow is honest but narrow, so please do not over-read it. Latency numbers from shared free compute are not an SLO. They describe a noisy shared path on one afternoon, and nothing more. Determinism claims need a seed you actually control. If your endpoint ignores the seed, count distinct outputs and stop pretending you have reproducibility. Skip this entirely if you need audited benchmarks. Pinned hardware, a fixed revision, and a signed methodology are a different project with a different budget. Skip it if your product is intentionally nondeterministic. A variance probe on a creative-writing assistant measures the product, not your prompt. Do not use it to compare vendors. Two logs from two providers will almost never share a revision namespace, and the comparison will be meaningless in exactly the way mine was. If you want to try the two-day loop before asking anyone for a budget, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option were enough for me to get the harness running, and I would start with the raw JSONL log rather than the summary table. Just add the revision guard before the first request, not after the first surprise.

title: How to Serve an LLM with an OpenAI-Compatible API on a Dedicated GPU Server
author: Thea Lauren
summary: Running a large language model on your own hardware gives you control over deployment, inference resources, and API access. With an OpenAI-compatible API , your applications can talk to a self-hosted model using the same client libraries and request formats you may already use. This post summarizes how to do it on a dedicated GPU server with vLLM , an open-source inference and serving engine. The full tutorial, with all commands and tables, is linked at the end. What "OpenAI-compatible" means vLLM exposes familiar endpoints: /v1/chat/completions for conversational requests /v1/completions for text generation from a prompt /v1/models to list available models One caveat: compatibility doesn't mean every OpenAI feature is available. Supported parameters depend on the inference engine and the model you deploy. Hardware: VRAM comes first GPU memory is the key constraint. You need room for the model weights, runtime overhead, and the KV cache. A 16-bit model needs roughly two bytes per parameter for raw weights alone, and real usage is higher. Size your GPU from the model's documented requirements and your expected workload, not parameter count alone. Install vLLM On Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, with a working NVIDIA driver (check with nvidia-smi ), create an isolated environment and install vLLM: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh mkdir ~/llm-server && cd ~/llm-server uv venv --python 3.12 --seed source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install vllm --torch-backend = auto Start the API server The tutorial uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as an example. Check that your GPU has enough VRAM before choosing a model. export MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct" export VLLM_API_KEY = "replace-with-a-long-random-secret" vllm serve " $MODEL_ID " \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 \ --dtype auto \ --max-model-len 4096 \ --api-key " $VLLM_API_KEY " Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the API off the public network, which is a safer starting point. Test it with the OpenAI Python SDK Because the API is compatible, you only change the base_url : import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI ( base_url = " http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 " , api_key = os . environ [ " VLLM_API_KEY " ] ) response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = " Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct " , messages = [ { " role " : " system " , " content " : " You are a helpful technical assistant. " }, { " role " : " user " , " content " : " Explain the benefits of dedicated GPU servers. " } ], temperature = 0.7 , max_tokens = 200 ) print ( response . choices [ 0 ]. message . content ) Security: don't rely on the API key alone To serve remote applications, put Nginx in front of vLLM, enable HTTPS, and restrict access with firewall rules. The --api-key option doesn't cover every endpoint on the HTTP server (the /invocations endpoint needs extra protection), so never expose an unrestricted inference endpoint to the public internet. Monitor and troubleshoot Watch GPU utilization, memory, temperature, power, request latency, and tokens per second with watch -n 2 nvidia-smi . If memory runs short, reduce context length, choose a smaller model, or use a supported quantization method. Read the full tutorial The complete walkthrough, including parameter tables and a troubleshooting section, is on the Leo Servers tutorial page: 👉 How to Serve an LLM with an OpenAI-Compatible API on a GPU Server Have you self-hosted an LLM before? Which inference engine did you use? Let me know in the comments.

title: Inherited Green: Freeze Debt Accounting for Agent Patches
author: Finley Zhou
summary: The conclusion first: an agent patch is not verified by the suite passing. It is verified by the assertions that executed in the head branch and did not execute in the base branch. Everything else is borrowed. Most agent pipelines report one bit: green or red. That bit hides two inflators. Skips inherited from the base branch silently shrink the evidence surface. Property tests that re-draw their randomness on every run make a pass non-reproducible by default. Fix both and the patch review gets shorter, not longer. This post is about accounting, not about catching flakes. Attribution work — deciding whether a patch caused a flake or merely surfaced one — is a separate gate. Here the question is narrower: how much of this green did the patch actually earn? 1. The failure mode, with a small trace The following trace is illustrative, not a benchmark. Base branch: 412 tests pass, 1 test frozen as FRZ-014 because it fails roughly 1 in 40 CI runs on a wall-clock boundary. Agent patch touches src/pricing/rounding.py , adds two tests, suite goes green at 414 executed. The delta looks like +2 . The riskiest changed line is covered by exactly the frozen test, which did not run. Nothing here is dishonest. The patch genuinely added two tests. The problem is that "+2" was reported without subtracting what the patch was already missing, and without noticing that the freeze covered the changed file. So the rule is not "no skips". It is: skips are fine, unaccounted skips are not, and a skip whose blast radius overlaps your diff is a blocker unless a compensating check runs in the same build. 2. Step 1 — make every skip auditable Add a session-level collector. It records executed and skipped node IDs with no plugin dependency, so it works the same in a container, a laptop, and a hosted runner. # conftest.py — run with: EVIDENCE_OUT=head.json pytest -q import json import os import pathlib _records = [] def pytest_runtest_logreport ( report ): # setup-phase skips and call-phase results are the only ones we count if report . when not in ( " setup " , " call " ): return if report . when == " call " or report . outcome == " skipped " : _records . append ( { " nodeid " : report . nodeid , " when " : report . when , " outcome " : report . outcome , # passed | failed | skipped # xfail reports as "skipped"; keep it separable " xfail " : getattr ( report , " wasxfail " , None ) is not None , } ) def pytest_sessionfinish ( session , exitstatus ): path = pathlib . Path ( os . environ . get ( " EVIDENCE_OUT " , " evidence.json " )) path . write_text ( json . dumps ({ " exit " : int ( exitstatus ), " records " : _records }, indent = 2 ), encoding = " utf-8 " , ) Run it twice, in the same image digest, against the same dependency lockfile: git worktree add /tmp/base " $( git merge-base origin/main HEAD ) " ( cd /tmp/base && EVIDENCE_OUT = /tmp/base.json pytest -q || true ) EVIDENCE_OUT = /tmp/head.json pytest -q || true Same image matters more than it sounds. A drifted dependency between the two runs produces a delta that measures the environment, not the patch. 3. Step 2 — compute the evidence delta The script below answers four questions: how many tests net executed, what skips are new, what previously passed and no longer does, and whether the diff touches a frozen blast radius. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ evidence_delta.py <base.json> <head.json> <freeze_ledger.toml> <today ISO> Adjust the git ref below to your integration branch. """ import json import subprocess import sys try : import tomllib # Python 3.11+ except ModuleNotFoundError : # 3.10 and older import tomli as tomllib def load ( path ): with open ( path , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as fh : data = json . load ( fh ) buckets = { " passed " : set (), " failed " : set (), " skipped " : set (), " xfail " : set ()} for r in data [ " records " ]: key = " xfail " if r [ " xfail " ] else r [ " outcome " ] buckets [ key ]. add ( r [ " nodeid " ]) return { " exit " : data [ " exit " ], ** buckets } def frozen_surface ( ledger_path , today ): with open ( ledger_path , " rb " ) as fh : ledger = tomllib . load ( fh ) return { path for entry in ledger . get ( " freeze " , []) if str ( entry [ " expires " ]) >= today # ISO dates compare lexicographically for path in entry [ " covers " ] } if __name__ == " __main__ " : base_path , head_path , ledger_path , today = sys . argv [ 1 : 5 ] base , head = load ( base_path ), load ( head_path ) introduced = head [ " skipped " ] - base [ " skipped " ] retired = base [ " skipped " ] - head [ " skipped " ] lost = base [ " passed " ] - head [ " passed " ] net = len ( head [ " passed " ]) - len ( base [ " passed " ]) changed = set ( subprocess . check_output ( [ " git " , " diff " , " --name-only " , " origin/main...HEAD " ], text = True ). split () ) hot = changed & frozen_surface ( ledger_path , today ) print ( f " net executed delta : { net : + d } " ) print ( f " new skips : { len ( introduced ) } " ) print ( f " retired skips : { len ( retired ) } " ) print ( f " previously passing : { len ( lost ) } no longer passing " ) print ( f " frozen surface hit : { sorted ( hot ) or ' none ' } " ) problems = [] if head [ " exit " ] != 0 : problems . append ( f " head suite exit { head [ ' exit ' ] } " ) if introduced : problems . append ( " patch-introduced skips need a ledger entry " ) if lost : problems . append ( " tests that passed on base no longer pass " ) if hot : problems . append ( " diff touches a frozen blast radius; compensating check required " ) for p in problems : print ( f " BLOCK: { p } " ) sys . exit ( 1 if problems else 0 ) A positive net number is not a pass. It is a number that still has to survive the block list. 4. Step 3 — the ledger that gives a freeze an owner and a deadline A freeze without a blast radius cannot be matched against a diff, and a freeze without an owner never ends. Fourteen days is a policy choice, not a measurement. # freeze_ledger.toml [[ freeze ]] id = "FRZ-014" test = "tests/test_pricing.py::test_rounding_boundary" covers = [ "src/pricing/rounding.py" ] # blast radius, not a guess owner = "finley" # a human, reviewed in the PR opened = 2026 -10-30 expires = 2026 -11-13 reason = "wall-clock boundary; fails ~1/40 CI runs, see run 8812" compensating_check = "tests/property/test_rounding.py::test_fee_monotonic" Three rules keep the ledger from rotting: covers must be file paths, because file paths are what git diff returns. A test name alone is not matchable. Renewal requires a new reason and evidence that the compensating check advanced. No silent re-freeze chains. Ledger edits are human-reviewed. An agent that can both introduce a skip and write its ledger entry has removed the control entirely. 5. Step 4 — two lanes for property checks Property tests are the natural compensating check for a frozen example-based test. They are also the easiest way to produce a green that nobody can reproduce, because the generator picks new inputs each run. Use two lanes over the same properties. # tests/property/test_rounding.py import os from decimal import Decimal import pytest from hypothesis import given , settings , strategies as st MONEY = st . decimals ( min_value = Decimal ( " 0 " ), max_value = Decimal ( " 100000 " ), places = 2 , allow_nan = False , allow_infinity = False , ) PINNED = settings ( derandomize = True , max_examples = 300 , deadline = None , database = None ) HUNT = settings ( max_examples = 2000 , deadline = None ) # keeps the example database LANE = os . environ . get ( " PROPERTY_LANE " , " pinned " ) CFG = PINNED if LANE == " pinned " else HUNT @CFG @given ( amount = MONEY ) def test_fee_is_bounded ( amount ): total = apply_fee ( amount ) # code under test assert total >= amount assert total - amount <= MAX_FEE Why both lanes: Pinned lane ( derandomize=True , empty example database) reproduces byte-for-byte on every run. It belongs in the patch gate, because a reviewer must be able to re-run it and see the same inputs. Hunting lane (unpinned, database enabled) explores. It belongs on a schedule, not on every patch, or it becomes the flake source you were trying to eliminate. When the hunting lane finds a counterexample, promote it: add a literal @example(Decimal("1234.56")) to the test. The pinned lane then replays it forever. A patch touching fee logic is expected to either add a promoted example or state why the invariant space did not grow. That is corpus growth as a reviewable artifact, not a coverage percentage. 6. Fixtures: hash them, do not read them Fixture changes are an evidence-surface change, not a code change. Diff them explicitly instead of relying on a reviewer to notice: git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD -- tests/fixtures tests/factories tests/conftest.py Any output triggers two requirements: human sign-off and a ledger entry with scope = "fixture" . You do not need to judge whether the new fixture is weaker. You need it to be visible. 7. Decision table Numbers below are illustrative; thresholds are policy, not measurements. Base passed Head passed New skips Frozen surface hit Verdict 412 412 0 none merge-eligible 412 409 0 none reject — evidence shrink, needs explanation 412 414 3 none merge-eligible if each skip is ledgered and unexpired 412 414 3 none reject — unledgered suppression 412 415 1 src/pricing/rounding.py merge-eligible only with the compensating property test executing in head 412 415 1 src/pricing/rounding.py reject if the freeze expired yesterday 8. Where a hosted agent loop fits This harness is deliberately boring to run: two pytest invocations in one image plus one script. The expensive part is the patch loop itself, not the accounting. MonkeyCode's free model access keeps that loop cheap enough to generate candidate patches in volume, and its free server option is one way to run the agent session and both evidence runs in the same hosted environment rather than splitting base and head across a laptop and a CI runner. Both availability claims are operator-supplied: no quotas, model names, hardware, or duration are asserted here, and the harness below is equally valid with a local model or no agent at all. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. 9. Limitations, and who should skip this Aggregate counts are gameable. A patch can add ten cheap tests and delete one expensive test and score +9 . Track the per-file delta, not just the total. Pinning removes exploration. The pinned lane alone will never find a new counterexample. If the hunting lane does not actually run on a schedule, the two-lane design is decoration. xfail is not skip . The collector separates them for a reason; merging them makes an expected failure look like suppression. Deletions are ambiguous. lost fires for obsolete tests too. That is intentional friction, not a bug — it forces a sentence of explanation in the PR. This is a pre-filter, not a proof. It does not replace mutation testing or deliberate fault injection. It is the cheap step that tells you whether the expensive step is worth running. Do not adopt this if your suite is under roughly twenty tests, if you have no flake history to freeze against, or if your CI has no budget for a second lane. In those cases the ledger is ceremony and the delta is noise. For a small patch queue, a plain diff review is honest and faster. Run the delta over your last twenty agent patches before adding any new tooling. The number that matters is not how many went green — it is how many the block list rejected, and whether you agreed with it. Code in this article is a sketch: the collector and delta script are written against standard pytest hooks and git diff , but you should expect to adjust the git ref, the ledger path, and the settings profiles to your repository before relying on any exit code.

title: Your Characterization Test Captured the Clock: Prove Stability Before You Pin a Golden Master
author: Dakota Huang
summary: A golden master test records exactly one run. That run happened once, in one locale, on one machine. If you pin it immediately, you freeze a coincidence. The suite goes green today and red at 03:00 in CI. This is the cheapest refactor failure to prevent. Prove the capture is deterministic, then pin it. 1. The Failure Mode: One Sample, Many Ambients Legacy code reads ambient state everywhere. Clocks, locales, timezones, hash seeds, filesystem order, environment variables. Your characterization test captures whatever those returned during recording. Every later run compares against that snapshot. Nothing in the test says which inputs were ambient. So a failure six weeks later looks like a refactor bug. It is usually a changed container timezone or a different LANG . 2. Build a Perturbation Matrix, Not a Bigger Fixture Do not guess which ambient inputs matter. Measure them. Step 1: list the perturbations you can reproduce cheaply. Timezone, locale, hash seed, working directory. Step 2: run the target function in a child process for each one. Twice per cell. Step 3: hash the serialized output. Compare hashes, never prose. Step 4: report which cells differ from baseline. That set is your volatility set. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ probe_stability.py — find ambient state a characterization test silently captured. """ import hashlib , json , os , subprocess , sys CHILD = r """ import importlib, json, sys module_path, fn_name, raw_arg = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3] fn = getattr(importlib.import_module(module_path), fn_name) print(json.dumps(fn(json.loads(raw_arg)), sort_keys=True, default=str)) """ PERTURBATIONS = [ ( " baseline " , {}), ( " tz_tokyo " , { " TZ " : " Asia/Tokyo " }), ( " tz_utc " , { " TZ " : " UTC " }), ( " locale_c " , { " LANG " : " C " , " LC_ALL " : " C " }), ( " hashseed_1 " , { " PYTHONHASHSEED " : " 1 " }), ( " hashseed_2 " , { " PYTHONHASHSEED " : " 2 " }), ] STRIPPED = { " PYTHONHASHSEED " , " TZ " , " LANG " , " LC_ALL " } def run_once ( module , fn , arg , extra_env ): env = { k : v for k , v in os . environ . items () if k not in STRIPPED } env . update ( extra_env ) proc = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , " -c " , CHILD , module , fn , json . dumps ( arg )], capture_output = True , text = True , env = env , timeout = 120 , ) if proc . returncode != 0 : last = proc . stderr . strip (). splitlines ()[ - 1 ][: 120 ] return " ERROR: " + last return hashlib . sha256 ( proc . stdout . strip (). encode ()). hexdigest ()[: 12 ] def main (): module , fn = sys . argv [ 1 ], sys . argv [ 2 ] arg = json . loads ( sys . argv [ 3 ]) if len ( sys . argv ) > 3 else {} rows = [] for name , extra in PERTURBATIONS : digests = [ run_once ( module , fn , arg , extra ) for _ in range ( 2 )] rows . append ({ " perturbation " : name , " runs " : digests , " stable_in_env " : digests [ 0 ] == digests [ 1 ], }) baseline = rows [ 0 ][ " runs " ][ 0 ] for r in rows : r [ " differs_from_baseline " ] = r [ " runs " ][ 0 ] != baseline print ( json . dumps ( rows , indent = 2 )) volatile = [ r [ " perturbation " ] for r in rows if r [ " differs_from_baseline " ] or not r [ " stable_in_env " ]] print ( " \n VOLATILE: " , " , " . join ( volatile ) or " none " , file = sys . stderr ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () Run it against the exact function your test plans to capture: python probe_stability.py orders.pricing quote '{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}' The stderr line is the only output you need to gate on. VOLATILE: none means you can pin. 3. Read the Report as Three Different Signals A cell that differs between two runs in the same environment is in-process nondeterminism. Reach for random , uuid , or iteration order. A cell that matches its twin but differs from baseline is ambient dependence. Reach for a pin. A cell that returns ERROR: is an environment trap, not a bug. Missing locale, unwritable path, absent config. Do not collapse these into one "flaky" bucket. Each has a different fix. 4. Decision Table for the Volatility Set Ambient input Cheapest honest fix Never do this Wall clock Inject a clock seam at the function boundary Call a freeze library inside business logic Timezone Set TZ in the test runner Format dates as strings earlier Locale, number format Pin LANG / LC_ALL in the runner Hardcode one separator in source Hash seed, set order Sort before serializing Sort inside production code uuid , secrets , tokens Stub at the call site the test owns Regex the value out of the snapshot Filesystem order Use tmp_path , seed the directory Assume os.listdir is stable Network, DB state Quarantine the test, fix the seam first Retry until green The rule is constant. Push the ambient control to the edge of the system, never into the logic you are about to refactor. 5. Pin Only Inside the Characterization Suite Scope the pins to the recording suite. Do not leak them into unit tests that should notice a real clock change. # tests/characterization/conftest.py import random import pytest @pytest.fixture ( autouse = True ) def pin_ambient ( monkeypatch , tmp_path ): monkeypatch . setenv ( " TZ " , " UTC " ) monkeypatch . setenv ( " LANG " , " C " ) monkeypatch . setenv ( " LC_ALL " , " C " ) monkeypatch . chdir ( tmp_path ) random . seed ( 0 ) yield One caveat matters here. PYTHONHASHSEED is read at interpreter start, so a fixture cannot change it. Set it in the runner instead, and verify it was actually applied: PYTHONHASHSEED = 0 pytest tests/characterization -p no:randomly -q Do not trust the variable blindly. Print os.environ.get("PYTHONHASHSEED") in one test and assert it. 6. Make the Smallest Safe Change, Then Re-Probe Now you can refactor. Extract one function. Change one call site. Keep the public signature untouched. After the edit, re-run the probe on the same inputs. Two numbers must hold. The VOLATILE set did not grow. The golden output is byte-identical, or every difference is explained in the commit message. A growth in the volatile set is a regression you caused. Fix it before the diff grows further. Keep the patch small enough to review in one sitting. Aggregate line counts before you request review: git diff --numstat -- src/legacy | awk '{a+=$1; d+=$2} END {print a" added, "d" deleted"}' If a file outside src/legacy changed, stop. That is a scope question, not a refactor. 7. Where Hosted Model Access Helped, and Where It Did Not This workflow is child-process heavy. Six perturbations times two runs, times every function you plan to capture. I ran those matrices on MonkeyCode's free server option so the loop did not occupy my laptop. I also used its free model access to draft the pinning fixture and the decision-table rows. Both availability claims are operator-supplied, so confirm the current limits yourself before relying on them. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The models were useful and wrong in equal measure. One proposed patching the clock deep inside the pricing function, which would have hidden the exact bug I was trying to freeze. I rejected it and moved the seam to the boundary. Treat generated pins as candidates. Every one needs a matching probe run before it enters the suite. 8. Limitations and Who Should Skip This This approach costs child processes. For a function taking a large binary input, the matrix is slow and the hashing is wasteful. It also assumes the legacy behavior is worth preserving. If the current output is the bug, a golden master locks the bug in. Characterize only what a caller depends on. Skip this if your target needs shared database state. Parallel child processes will collide, and the probe results become noise. Skip it too when the suite already runs under a fixed container image. Half the matrix is then a no-op, and you can check TZ and hash seed by inspection. Finally, this proves determinism, not correctness. A stable wrong answer is still wrong. The Two-Line Test Before you pin any golden master, ask two questions. Does it reproduce twice in the same environment? Does it survive a timezone change? If either answer is no, the snapshot is a coin flip. Fix the ambient input first, then refactor with confidence. Run the probe on your least favorite module this week. The VOLATILE line is usually shorter than you fear and more surprising than you expect.

title: Keeping a game widget from eating CPU when 40 tabs are open
author: haibo kan
summary: This is a follow-up to my earlier write-up, Injecting a game widget into every page without breaking the host site's CSS . That one covered style isolation. This one is about lifecycle, which turned out to be the harder half. The product constraint sounds innocuous: a small draggable ball sits in the corner of every page, you click it, pick a game, press Space, and click again to fold it away. The part that matters is the last step — folding it away pauses the game and keeps the state, so you come back to the same round. If you take that literally on every tab, you have 40 game loops. That's the design problem. The widget is everywhere; the game is not The content script that mounts the ball is tiny: one host element, a Shadow DOM root, a drag handler. It does no work when idle. The game itself doesn't exist until you pick one. When you pick a game, an iframe is created on demand, the game bundle loads into it, and the loop starts. When you switch games or collapse the panel, the iframe is destroyed. There is no persistent background page holding a loop, and no service worker ticking on a timer. That gives a useful invariant: the number of running game loops is at most one per active widget, and usually zero. Forty tabs means forty tiny idle elements, not forty requestAnimationFrame loops. Three different kinds of "pause" I initially lumped everything under "auto-pause", and it caused bugs, because the three cases have different semantics: Collapse / Esc — an explicit user action. Freeze immediately and keep the state. This is the one people notice, and the one that has to feel instant. Tab hidden — the browser already throttles requestAnimationFrame in background tabs. I don't need to tear anything down; a loop driven by rAF naturally stops advancing. Fighting the browser here just adds a state-restore bug. Switching games — this is not a pause at all. Tear down the iframe and start clean. Keeping a hidden game alive "just in case" is what creates the 40-loop problem in the first place. Separating those three removed most of the state bugs I had early on. Store the smallest thing that can restore a round The tempting approach is to serialize the whole game object. Don't. Most of it is derived state — sprite positions, timers, DOM nodes — and rehydrating it is both brittle and pointless. What actually needs to survive: { score : 120 , level : 3 , grid : [...], // board state only direction : ' right ' , nextDirection : ' right ' , tick : 1840 // logical ticks elapsed, not wall-clock ms } tick instead of Date.now() matters. If your speed curve is derived from elapsed wall-clock time, a round that sat paused for twenty minutes comes back at a different difficulty from the one you left. A logical counter that only advances inside the loop doesn't have that problem. The other trap is writing on every frame. chrome.storage.local is not a frame buffer. I write on pause, on game over, and on a coarse interval — never inside the loop. Click-through is a pointer-events problem with one exception "Click-through mode" means the widget stops intercepting your mouse entirely, so it never steals a click from the page underneath. The obvious implementation is pointer-events: none on the widget surface. The exception is the drag handle: it still needs pointer events while everything else doesn't. So the handle keeps pointer-events: auto and the rest is disabled as a layer, rather than toggling one global flag and then wondering why the ball can't be moved anymore. What I'd do differently Two things: I treated "paused" as one state for too long. Collapse, background tab and game switch are three different transitions and should have been three code paths from day one. I should have designed the save-state shape before the game code. Deciding what to serialize after the fact means the game object leaks into storage and you end up versioning a format nobody designed. None of this is novel — it's the same lifecycle discipline you'd apply to any embedded widget. It's just easy to forget when the thing you're embedding happens to be a game. If you want to see it in practice, the extension is called InTab Arcade. Three games are free with no account; a retro arcade cabinet is a paid upgrade.

title: GEO Generative Engine Optimization Guide: The Complete 2026 Strategy
author: GrowGanic
summary: A GEO generative engine optimization guide is the essential playbook for structuring your content so AI answer engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews cite it in their responses. This guide covers the complete strategy from audit to execution. If you are still optimizing only for Google's 10 blue links, you're invisible to half your potential customers. Generative engine optimization ( GEO ) is the practice of structuring digital content and managing online presence to improve visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence Wikipedia. Traditional SEO optimized for a list of links. GEO optimizes for a single synthesized answer. This guide walks you through every layer, from the technical signals that AI crawlers care about to the content structure that makes extraction easy. What is Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)? What Exactly Is a GEO Generative Engine Optimization Guide? A GEO generative engine optimization guide is a structured resource that teaches you how to make your content citeable by AI-powered search engines. It covers the research, content structuring, technical optimization, and monitoring required to appear in AI-generated answers. The core definition comes from Wikipedia: GEO is "the practice of structuring digital content and managing online presence to improve visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence" Wikipedia. This is broader than SEO because the target is no longer a list of URLs, it is a single synthesized paragraph or answer block. How GEO Differs from Traditional SEO Traditional SEO optimized for rankings in a list of blue links. GEO optimizes for extractability by large language models (LLMs). AI answer engines do not "read" pages the way humans do. They scan for clear, structured facts that can be lifted into a generated answer. Semrush defines GEO as "the practice of optimizing your presence and content to appear in responses generated by AI-powered search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity." This means the same content must satisfy both a human reader and an AI extraction mechanism. The two are not always aligned. Why GEO Matters More Than SEO in 2026 Why Is Generative Engine Optimization Important for 2026? A 2023 Pew Research Center survey found that 55% of U.S. adults have used an AI chatbot or virtual assistant to search for information. That number is only rising. AI Overviews now appear above traditional organic results on Google itself, and standalone AI answer engines like ChatGPT and Perplexity are growing fast. If your content is not structured for AI extraction, you are invisible in these answers. Competitors who optimize for GEO capture the traffic that used to flow through organic links. The shift is permanent. What Does the Data Say About AI Search Adoption? The direction is clear: appearing in AI-generated answers matters more every year for commercial and professional queries. The academic community is also paying attention. Pan et al. (2026) published a paper titled "Generative Engine Optimization (GEO): The Architecture of Visibility in AI-Mediated Discovery" Crossref. Quintana-Gómez et al. (2026) explored GEO and brand visibility in AI-generated tourism recommendations Revista Prisma Social. This is not a passing trend. How AI Answer Engines Actually Choose Sources How Do AI Search Engines Decide Which Sources to Cite? AI models do not "read" pages like humans. They extract facts from structured content. Pages with clear headings, concise definitions, and high information density are more likely to be cited. Fluff and vague marketing language hurt your chances. For the exact signals Google weighs when it builds an answer, see our breakdown of how AI Overviews pick sources . Content freshness is a major factor. Research cited by Directive Consulting shows that AI assistants exhibit a recency bias. Content older than three months receives significantly fewer citations in AI-generated responses Directive Consulting. This means the "set it and forget it" approach to content kills your GEO performance. What Role Does Recency Play in AI Citations? Recency is critical. Directive Consulting recommends refreshing high-value pages at least quarterly. This is not optional for GEO. We map the full citation decay curve in content freshness and AI citations . LLMrefs adds that AI systems often break complex user questions into multiple sub-queries, known as fan-out queries LLMrefs. To rank well in GEO, you must optimize for these smaller component queries as well as the main topic. This multiplies the surface area you need to cover. Technical performance also matters. Strapi's 2025 GEO guide explains that Core Web Vitals like Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and Time to First Byte (TTFB) remain critical because AI bots often abandon slow-loading pages Strapi. A slow page reduces crawl coverage and citation likelihood. The 4-Phase GEO Framework That Actually Works What Is the GEO Optimization Process? The most effective GEO approach follows a four-phase cycle: source analysis, optimization, assessment, and refinement. It is the workflow the AI visibility monitoring category converges on, and you can see how those AI visibility tools compare . We have adapted it into a practical process that fits any team size. The cycle starts with auditing your current AI visibility. Track 25 to 100 relevant prompts daily for at least one week to map where your brand appears across AI platforms. A disciplined prompt audit is the starting point. Once you know where you stand, you can fix what is broken. Content structure is the next lever. Clear headings, concise definitions, and cited statistics make your pages easy for AI to extract. Remove fluff. Every sentence should either define something, prove something, or guide the reader to the next point. Nothing else earns its place on the page. After the content is clean, the technical signals matter. Schema markup, fast load times, and a clear freshness schedule are table stakes for GEO. Skip any of these and you are handing citations to a competitor who did not skip them. Then you monitor and iterate, because AI answer engines change their citation patterns regularly. A page that gets cited today may lose visibility next month if a fresher or more structured version appears somewhere else. This is exactly the loop we automated inside GrowGanic. The pipeline handles the audit, the optimization, and the refresh without a human touching it. How to Audit Your Current AI Visibility Start with a manual prompt audit. Track 25 to 100 prompts relevant to your industry each day for a week. Note which domains and URLs are cited. Look for patterns in content structure and freshness. Tools like Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit can help track share of voice across AI platforms. But manual analysis gives you immediate insight into why your content is or is not being cited. Why Content Structure Matters for AI Extraction AI engines pull facts from clear, self-contained statements. A paragraph that mixes a definition with a marketing pitch is less extractable than a bolded definition followed by separate supporting points. Use definition lists, numbered takeaways, and short summary boxes. Each piece of content should have one primary claim that an AI can extract cleanly. How to Do GEO Optimization: A Step-by-Step Process Audit your current AI footprint. Use a prompt-tracking audit to identify where you are cited and where you are missing. Identify high-value queries. Focus on queries where a citation would drive traffic or conversions. These are the questions your target audience asks AI engines. Restructure content for extractability. Bold key claims. Use definition format for core terms. Add structured data. JSON-LD for FAQ, HowTo, and Article schema helps AI engines understand your page structure. This is a direct signal for citation. Implement a freshness schedule. Directive Consulting recommends quarterly refreshes for high-value pages Directive Consulting. Update statistics, add new context, and republish with a prominent last-updated date. Monitor citations and iterate. Use dedicated GEO tracking tools to see when your citations change. Adjust your content structure and topics based on what the AI engines are citing. Or you can skip steps 1-6 and let GrowGanic do them. More on that later. Which Technical Signals Improve AI Citation Likelihood? Core Web Vitals are the foundation. Fast load times reduce abandonment by AI crawlers. Schema markup gives AI engines structured context about your content. FAQ schema, HowTo schema, and Article schema are the most impactful for GEO. A clear content freshness signal, a prominent "last updated" date and regular republishing, fights the recency bias that Directive Consulting identified. What Industry Authorities Report About GEO Performance What Do GEO Benchmarks Tell Us? Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit measures share of voice across AI platforms. They track brand mentions, sentiment, and citation frequency. Early benchmarks show that structured, fresh content receives 3x to 5x more citations than unstructured or stale content. The monitoring playbook recommends continuous prompt tracking to build a baseline. GEO performance is not static. How to Apply Recency Research from Directive Consulting Directive content older than three months sees a measurable drop in AI citations Directive Consulting. This recency bias is built into how LLMs weigh sources. The fix is a regular refresh cadence. Update statistics, add new sections, and republish with a new date. This signals to the AI that the content is current and increases citation likelihood. GEO vs. Traditional SEO: What Changes and What Stays What Is the Difference Between SEO and GEO? Dimension Traditional SEO GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) Goal Rank in Google's 10 blue links Get cited in AI-generated answers Content structure Keyword-focused paragraphs Extractable fact-focused structure Freshness Nice-to-have, often ignored Critical for citation likelihood Technical signals Important for ranking Table-stakes, without them AI bots abandon the page Audience Human searchers clicking links AI engines extracting facts Success metric Organic traffic and keyword positions Citation frequency and share of voice in AI answers GEO does not replace SEO. It layers on top. A page that ranks #1 in Google but is not extractable by AI loses half its potential traffic. For a full side by side, read GEO vs SEO . Which Approach Should You Prioritize in 2026? You need both. But if you have limited resources, prioritize GEO first. AI-generated answers are appearing above traditional organic results in many verticals. Getting cited in an AI answer gives you visibility that a traditional ranking cannot match. GrowGanic scores for both Google readiness and AI-search readiness in a single pass. The system evaluates content against both dimensions simultaneously. Common GEO Mistakes That Kill Your AI Visibility What Are the Most Common GEO Mistakes? The most common mistake is writing for humans only. Long paragraphs with buried claims are hard for AI to extract. You need bold definitions, clear structure, and concise statements. The subtler trap is ignoring recency. Publishing a piece of content once and never refreshing it guarantees that it will stop getting cited within a few months. Directive Consulting's recency bias data shows this clearly Directive Consulting. Neglecting technical performance is the expensive failure. Slow pages get skipped by AI crawlers, and Strapi's guide makes clear that Core Web Vitals are not optional for GEO Strapi. You can have the most extractable content on the web and still lose citations because your server is slow. The overlooked mistake is not optimizing for fan-out queries. AI breaks complex questions into multiple sub-queries LLMrefs. If you only optimize for the main query, you miss every sub-query where AI could have cited you instead of a competitor. The refresh runs on a schedule you never touch: the engine re-checks the statistics, rewrites the weakest sections, and republishes with a fresh last-updated date while you sleep. Recency stops being a chore you forget and becomes a property of the system. That is the whole point of treating GEO as an engine instead of a checklist. You map the territory once.
